notes: A conference abstract or presentation can offer early findings with limited methods; inspect any poster or slides separately. A preprint is a versioned manuscript released before completed journal peer review. A full article usually permits more inspection, including its supplement, protocol and analysis plan, but can still have missing information or exploratory analyses. An abstract may also be the summary of a full article, so its existence does not make evidence conference-only. Editorial peer review, conference selection and independent replication are different forms of scrutiny, and newer does not automatically mean better designed. A study report, news release and commentary are different source types.

Keep the study identifier, document type, date and version, recruited population, denominator, endpoint and starting clock, data cutoff and follow-up, analysis role and location of methods. Check corrections and retractions at the publisher and inspect the affected claim. ICMJE recommends a correction notice detailing changes, a dated updated version and an archive of prior versions. A full paper with an abstract and later correction should be identified as that sequence, not called conference-only. This checking sequence makes limitations visible; it does not certify validity.

Fictional publication example: an early report describes 12 responses among 20 participants, while a later full report includes 30 participants and longer follow-up. Both can be accurate for their cutoffs. Do not combine the early response percentage with the later follow-up as one estimate, or treat overlapping participants as independent confirmation. New methods or comparator details can change interpretation, but publishing a single-group study in full does not create a randomized control group.

records.name: Radioligand dosimetry
records.tldr: Radioligand dosimetry estimates radiation deposited in tumors and normal tissues from where radioactivity goes and how it changes with time.
records.summary: Calibrated activity measurements, often from suitable serial SPECT or PET imaging, inform a time-activity model. Time-integrated decays, emission properties, tissue mass and spatial assumptions then inform absorbed dose. Equal uptake on an early scan can be followed by different retention and different doses. Administered activity is an input, not a substitute for patient- or tissue-level dosimetry. The estimates can support evaluation of dosing strategies, but improved outcomes from a particular adaptation require their own evidence.

notes: Physical decay, biological clearance and radioactive daughters all affect interpretation. Alpha-emitter dosimetry may need additional microscopic considerations. FDA’s cited document addresses nonclinical development; it is not a universal clinical dosing protocol or evidence of a jurisdiction-wide reimbursement requirement.

Absorbed dose in gray (Gy) is energy deposited per tissue mass, with 1 Gy equal to 1 joule per kilogram. Administered activity in MBq measures radioactive decays per time, not energy absorbed. A single uptake image or SUV is neither quantity. Dose estimation needs an appropriate time-activity model, emissions and energy-deposition assumptions for the relevant tissue. Equal early uptake can precede different retention. The tested diagnostic tracer cannot supply a different therapeutic product's dose merely because both bind the same target.
records.principle: Estimate activity through time in specified source regions, then calculate the energy deposited in relevant target regions with explicit assumptions.
strengths: Makes tumor and normal-tissue exposure explicit
Can evaluate why the same administered activity produces different dose estimates
limitations: Calibration, time sampling and segmentation affect estimates
Organ averages can miss uneven microscopic exposure
Method-specific dose estimates do not establish a universal clinical threshold

records.name: Radioligand therapy (beta emitters)
records.tldr: A target-binding molecule carries a radionuclide whose emissions deposit radiation in tissue. Distribution and retention help determine tumor and normal-organ exposure.
records.summary: Lutetium-177 therapies deliver beta-particle radiation through target-binding molecules. VISION tested PSMA-targeted treatment added to protocol-permitted standard care in selected, previously treated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. NETTER-1 tested lutetium-177-dotatate in progressive, somatostatin-receptor-positive midgut neuroendocrine tumors. Their clinical results belong to those populations and products, rather than every tumor expressing the target. Small molecules, peptides and antibodies have different distribution and clearance even when directed at a shared target.

notes: Radioactive activity is a decay rate in becquerels; absorbed dose is deposited energy per mass in gray. A single bright image is not time-integrated exposure. Dosimetry combines suitable activity measurements or models over time with tissue geometry and emission properties. Neither the targeting-molecule mass nor the administered activity alone specifies tumor dose.

Radioimmunotherapy uses an antibody carrier. The broader radiopharmaceutical category also includes organ-seeking products without a separate targeting ligand. Not every attachment uses a metal chelator. Alpha and beta emissions have different path and energy-deposition properties; neither label alone ranks safety or effectiveness. Daughter redistribution and microscopic geometry can matter.

Radiation can deposit energy beyond the cell carrying the radioactive product, so chemical-payload uptake into each neighbouring cell is not the same requirement. Binding and internalisation can affect retention, but the complete carrier's distribution, biological removal, radionuclide decay and tissue geometry still determine delivery. A diagnostic tracer image is not a measured therapeutic absorbed dose, and resistance to a chemotherapy payload does not itself establish radiation sensitivity or safe organ exposure.

Sgouros's 2020 review labels its table values approximate emission range in tissue: 0.62 mm for lutetium-177 beta emission, and 0.05 to 0.08 mm for the listed radium-223, actinium-225 and thorium-227 alpha emitters. That column does not identify the values as mean or maximum ranges, so they should not silently be relabelled as either or used as exact treatment boundaries. The isotope and range convention matter; one beta or alpha number is not a value for every radionuclide. FDA's 2019 radiopharmaceutical guidance separately defines physical, biological and effective half-life and time-integrated activity.
records.principle: Where the complete radioactive product travels, how long it remains and which emissions reach tissue jointly determine radiation delivery.
strengths: Targeted delivery of radiation through an accessible molecular feature
Emitted particles can reach neighboring cells
limitations: Kidney, marrow and other normal-tissue exposure can limit treatment
A positive scan alone does not establish absorbed dose or clinical benefit
Results from one radionuclide or carrier do not establish equivalence of another

records.name: Radiotherapy
records.tldr: Radiotherapy deposits ionising radiation in tissue to damage cancer cells. The target, normal tissues, treatment schedule and clinical goal all matter.
records.summary:
Radiation transfers energy to tissue and can damage DNA directly or through reactive molecules. Cells can repair damage or lose their ability to keep dividing, and death can occur later. One treatment session is an exposure, rather than an immediate count of dead cells. Oxygen, cell state and repair affect the response.

External beams, brachytherapy sources and systemically distributed radiopharmaceuticals have different exposure patterns. An external-beam target can include tissue at risk of microscopic disease after surgery, even when no mass is visible. Planning and verification consider geometry, motion, normal organs and previous overlapping exposure. Precision does not eliminate normal-tissue dose or injury.

Absorbed dose in gray is energy per mass: one gray is one joule per kilogram. Total dose, fraction size, timing and exposed volume influence biological effects. Physical-dose arithmetic alone does not establish equivalence of schedules. Local or regional control, symptom relief, distant disease and survival remain distinct clinical outcomes.

records.name: Randomised trial
records.tldr: A study that assigns eligible participants to interventions by chance. This reduces treatment-selection bias but does not guarantee identical groups, flawless follow-up or benefit.
records.summary: A randomized trial assigns eligible consenting participants to interventions by chance. Concealing the next assignment protects enrolment against foreknowledge; blinding concerns awareness after assignment. These are different design features. Randomization reduces treatment-selection confounding but leaves possible chance imbalance, missing outcomes and limits on applicability. The comparator, endpoint, analysis and conduct determine what the comparison establishes.

notes: Concealed chance assignment is different from predictable alternation between A and B. Allocation concealment hides the next assignment during enrolment; blinding concerns who knows the assigned treatment afterwards and may not be feasible for every intervention. Report sequence generation, allocation, who was blinded, assigned-group analyses, exclusions, dropout, missing assessments, treatment changes and unequal follow-up. Chance can balance measured and unmeasured factors on average without guaranteeing identical groups in one trial. Random assignment is not random sampling from a population: consenting eligible volunteers remain selected.

Controls can be standard care, standard care plus placebo or another protocol-defined option, not automatically no treatment. A fictional single-group Drug A study showing shrinkage supports an activity question for further study; it does not isolate added survival benefit from selection, natural history and other care. A randomized A-plus-usual-care versus usual-care comparison can test the added effect under sound conduct and analysis, while a volunteer cannot choose their randomized assignment or be promised benefit. A chance-assigned two-group phase 2 trial is randomized even though it is not phase 3.

records.name: RNA
records.tldr: RNA is a family of molecules with several jobs. Messenger RNA provides a protein-making template; other RNAs help build, regulate or carry out cellular processes.
records.summary: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

A noncoding RNA can function without becoming a protein, and reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant biological contexts. RNA amount does not determine a fixed protein amount or activity.

After successful delivery, a supplied ordinary mRNA can be translated at cytoplasmic ribosomes; that translation step does not require the message to enter the nucleus. Supplying a message, measuring endogenous tumor RNA and demonstrating nuclear DNA modification are separate observations. The NHGRI vaccine example illustrates supplied RNA instructions, not a general cancer-efficacy claim.

records.name: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT / SABR)
records.tldr: Stereotactic body radiotherapy delivers a high dose per treatment to a defined body target using specialised localisation and verification. A short schedule alone does not identify it or establish safety.
records.summary:
Stereotactic body radiotherapy, also called SABR, uses specialised localisation, planning, positioning, image guidance and delivery to give a high dose per fraction to a body target outside the brain. A small number of visits does not establish that this delivery package was used. A biologically effective dose calculation compares modelled effects under assumptions; it does not document stereotactic localisation, motion management or verification. Modern non-stereotactic radiotherapy can also use imaging, conformal beams and motion assessment.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Planned exposure, verified delivery, local control and toxicity need their own measurements.

A 2010 prospective study concerned medically inoperable peripheral early-stage lung cancer and measured local control, distant failure and toxicity. That setting does not validate treatment of every central lesion or organ. CURB and NRG-BR002 tested different metastatic settings and comparisons. Local control, added progression-free or overall survival, symptom relief and an immune response are separate outcomes.

records.name: Systemic versus local therapy
records.tldr: Local and regional treatments act in selected anatomical areas; systemic treatments circulate more broadly. The route does not guarantee adequate exposure or cancer control at every site.
records.summary:
Surgery, ablation and external radiation address defined tissues, while systemically administered medicines and radiopharmaceuticals distribute more broadly. Regional delivery has an intermediate anatomical scope. Distribution, effective exposure and benefit are separate questions; neither local nor systemic is a guarantee of complete cellular coverage.

Local control, distant progression, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief should be measured separately. A null added-survival comparison does not make palliation irrelevant, and a controlled treated site does not establish control throughout the body. Compare the actual complete strategies rather than assuming that adding a local method always improves outcomes.

notes: BOOSTER studied ablation during ongoing immunotherapy after limited residual lung disease; CURB studied SBRT for oligoprogression in lung and breast cohorts; NRG-BR002 studied ablation during first-line systemic treatment for limited metastatic breast cancer. PACIFIC tested consolidation durvalumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy in nonprogressing stage III lung cancer. These are distinct settings and intervention contrasts.

Start with the goal and history before choosing a clock. A smaller lesion is a response observation at assessment; local control concerns keeping that site from progressing during follow-up. Postoperative local-recurrence prevention, relief of pain from a bone metastasis and a growing lesion during otherwise controlled metastatic disease are different questions. A meaningful pain improvement need not wait for an untreated tumour to shrink. A positive blood molecular test does not identify a lesion's position, boundary or safe access. An earlier scan date alone does not demonstrate improved outcomes. These distinctions organise evidence review rather than select a dose, procedure or treatment date. Nonmetastatic disease means no established distant metastases; a stage and subtype still need their own comparison of local and systemic care. Recovery, healing, previous exposure, overlapping toxicities and protocol assessment times supply other clocks. They are reasons to examine the studied sequence rather than invent a universal interval or repeat a procedure whenever a blood marker rises.

A local-treatment proposal needs five connected answers: the local and hoped-for wider outcomes with their measurements; evidence matching the cancer, disease history, complete strategy and comparator; access, intended coverage, margins, motion and nearby structures; actual exposure and normal-tissue risk; and alternatives, burdens and remaining uncertainty. In a fictional pair of equally sized lesions, proximity to a sensitive airway and a different approach can change feasibility. Depth alone is also insufficient: some deep lesions can be accessed, while a superficial lesion can have a difficult margin. Small diameter and a positive tracer scan settle none of the wider immune or outcome claims. Comparators can include systemic treatment alone, another local strategy, observation where appropriate or a study; include visits, recovery and additional sampling among the burdens. For a tracer and therapeutic product, establish the relationship between them rather than treating target uptake as a measured therapeutic dose. This review identifies missing facts and does not authorise treatment.

Delivery can be compared without ranking treatments. A fictional probe card controls a selected liver site, a beam card specifies a lung volume and motion assessment, and a radioactive-drug card requires distribution, retention and organ dosimetry. They are different routes, not a ladder from one lesion to invisible disease. A systemically distributed radioactive product still does not guarantee exposure of every microscopic deposit. Radiation injury does not require a conventional T cell to recognise peptide-HLA; proposed antigen-specific immune effects still need presentation, access, recognition and function. In another invented study, people receiving the same systemic strategy are randomised to a local addition or no local addition. With the same defined progression endpoint, starting time and follow-up, treated sites are controlled but new lesions occur in both arms and the progression-free-survival interval spans effects in both directions. That supports local control while leaving the added progression effect uncertain; survival, quality of life, pain and harms remain separate outcomes.

PACIFIC's five-year report concerns durvalumab versus placebo after concurrent platinum-based chemoradiation in unresectable, nonprogressing stage III non-small-cell lung cancer. The report found sustained progression-free and overall-survival benefit for that tested consolidation strategy. It did not require stereotactic body radiation, identify an abscopal mechanism or establish that focused radiation should always precede checkpoint treatment across cancers. Randomised comparisons, development phase and publication format answer different questions; these study cards cannot rank technologies from separate headlines. A case can describe a clinical course, a nonrandomised comparison can be distorted by treatment selection, and a model can supply a rationale for testing. These designs do not establish the same causal claim.

records.name: T-cell receptor
records.tldr: A conventional T-cell receptor recognises a peptide together with its HLA display. Recognition alone does not show killing.
records.summary:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

notes: A conventional alpha-beta TCR uses paired variable and constant domains to contact peptide plus HLA. The peptide sits in the HLA groove, not a separate TCR peptide pocket. CD3 signalling partners are distinct from recognition chains. Contact loops including junction-spanning CDR3 contribute, but other loops, the partner chain and HLA matter; beta-only or CDR3-only sequence is incomplete.

Cross-reactivity is recognition of multiple targets by a receptor. Defined receptor experiments demonstrated peptide/HLA cross-reactivity, not recognition of every allele by an arbitrary receptor or a universal rate. Greater affinity or a contact drawing does not establish healthy-tissue safety.

Sequencing reports sampled receptor identities and abundances under an operational clonotype definition. Paired alpha-beta identities are more complete than beta alone. Peptide-HLA multimer binding, stimulus-induced cellular response, target-cell death and clinical benefit are different endpoints. Include irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls; peptide-loaded cells can bypass natural processing.

Vaccination generally recruits or expands existing mature receptor specificities rather than rewriting each mature receptor. Engineered TCR therapy introduces selected receptor sequences. In either case, tested recognition must still connect to naturally presenting tumour targets, useful function and healthy-tissue safety. If one beta sequence pairs with different alpha chains, a positive reconstruction of one pair does not establish the other pair's function or tumour killing.

Source scope: teaching synthesis checked against the cited abstracts and specified accessible primary text on 9 November 2026; fictional examples are not clinical observations or treatment-selection rules.

Many measured conventional receptor-peptide-HLA interactions have micromolar dissociation constants; affinity, multiple contacts, CD4/CD8 coreceptors and the cellular signalling context contribute differently to activity. Stone and colleagues review those distinctions, rather than a universal affinity ranking against every antibody. One receptor type per cell is also a simplification: extra productive alpha chains and dual surface receptors have been documented. A chain sequence alone does not establish which assembled receptor provides the measured specificity.

records.name: Targeted therapy
records.tldr: A targeted treatment acts on a specified molecule or process. Some block a cancer dependence; others use a molecule as an address for delivery or immune recruitment. The target name alone does not establish benefit or normal-tissue safety.
records.summary:
Targeted treatments include small molecules and therapeutic antibodies with different actions. A molecule whose function supports cancer growth and a surface molecule used to deliver an active drug or recruit an immune cell have different roles. Detecting either does not by itself establish that the finished treatment reaches its target, changes a relevant function or helps in a particular clinical setting.

Some treatments require a specified biomarker test; others have no target-expression selection test in the relevant label. Keep the actual drug, disease, treatment setting and testing rule together. NCI describes resistance and potentially serious adverse effects of targeted therapy. Neither relative normal-tissue sparing, mild toxicity nor a permanent response follows from the word targeted.

notes: Target, mechanism and evidence. A drug target is the molecule or structure a treatment acts on, and its mechanism of action is how that action produces an effect; a target name does not show that the target is reachable, required by the cancer, or that changing it does useful work. Binding to a purified protein, engagement in the relevant cell (the cellular thermal shift assay was introduced to evaluate drug binding in cells and tissues), a measured effect with controls, and benefit and harm in a stated clinical setting each need their own evidence, and a blood concentration is not the concentration at an intracellular target. In-cell thermal profiling can pick up indirect as well as direct targets (Ball et al. 2020). If an antibody is shown to bind a protein on cancer cells and growth is unchanged, binding is supported; dependence on the protein, inhibition of its function, delivery by a finished payload-bearing product, safety and benefit are not. A molecule used as an address for delivery and a molecule whose function the cell depends on are different roles.

What NCI says about the class. Targeted therapy was once expected to be less toxic than chemotherapy but can cause serious side effects, cancer cells can become resistant to it, and it may work best combined with other targeted therapy or with treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation (NCI page, HTML read).

A product proposal identifies the clinical problem, disease setting, treatment intent, alternatives and measurable goal; the exact target, specimen and method; accessible protein or peptide-HLA presentation and normal-tissue evidence with sampling limits; and the complete binder, linker, payload or cell design and mechanism. It records the relevant human comparison or explicitly limited preclinical evidence, product-specific safety monitoring, management capability and stopping rules. Keep manufacture, quality release, sponsor, site and access pathway separate from benefit. Reviewing existing data, consuming tissue for an experiment, manufacturing and administering treatment are different commitments with their own rationale and responsible owner. A target shortlist or recipe analogy establishes none of their benefit or safety.

Questions follow the product. For a cytotoxic antibody-drug conjugate, assess antibody, linker and payload together, delivery and exposure, tested resistance steps and the design-specific role of internalisation; FDA's March 2024 clinical-pharmacology guidance has this scope. For an engager or cell product, ask about cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity and other neurologic effects, healthy-tissue recognition, tissue access and what can persist after dosing stops. FDA's January 2024 CAR T-cell guidance describes product-specific recognition, expansion, persistence and toxicity management; it does not supply incidence for every engager. For a radioligand, ask how the imaging relates to that therapeutic product's distribution, organ absorbed doses and organ limits. FDA's August 2019 document addresses nonclinical studies and labeling, not a universal clinical dose threshold. Tracer uptake supplies no CAR-T safety threshold. For a T-cell-receptor proposal, ask which peptide-HLA target is recognised and how specificity, natural presentation and function were tested; receptor sequences or expanded clones alone leave these questions open.

Product Q is a fictional investigational conjugate against surface protein M, with a specified antibody, cleavable linker and cell-damaging payload. Adults with progressing metastatic solid cancer after prior treatment are the setting, and the immediate proposal is to review existing data before designing a laboratory experiment. No manufacture, treatment or new sample collection is proposed. The dossier has M RNA measurements from one tumour biopsy and Q activity in target-bearing cultured cells, without direct surface measurement, relevant healthy-tissue tests or a human comparison. Supplier participation, access and site arrangements are unknown. These findings support a research hypothesis about Q, not demonstrated clinical benefit or evidence borrowed from another M-targeted format.

Complete the fictional Q card by retaining accessible tumour protein, healthy-tissue effects, full-product delivery and relevant human outcomes as missing evidence. A research lead first reviews methods, controls and Q-specific product data; this existing-data review consumes no tissue. Pause experiment planning if product identity or usable evidence remains unavailable, and ask which Q-specific result would change the experiment plan. RNA abundance is a different observation from accessible surface protein. Mertins and colleagues measured RNA, protein and phosphoprotein layers in primary breast cancers; that work is not a cell-surface-accessibility or treatment-selection assay. Confirming protein would answer another premise while leaving benefit unproven.

Now change only the fictional request: after complete tumour removal, someone proposes manufacturing Q and administering it to prevent recurrence because M RNA was abundant, an IND is said to be active and a supplier offers manufacture. The setting and commitments have changed, while the dossier is still one biopsy RNA signal plus cultured-cell activity. Neither that evidence nor the attributed investigational milestone or supply offer establishes postoperative benefit. Ask the clinical team for Q-specific human evidence or a relevant protocol, the sponsor which product and protocol are covered, and the readiness owner about delivery requirements. In the United States an effective Investigational New Drug application is not marketing approval, and submission of a Biologics License Application is not its approval. A manufacturing quote cannot confirm supply, consent, review, delivery and monitoring as a whole. With only this dossier, evidence and pathway review are justified; manufacture or administration is not justified by the supplied information. Speculative availability does not promise access or protection against recurrence.

records.name: Thermal ablation (RFA, microwave, cryo)
records.tldr: Thermal ablation uses an applicator to heat or freeze selected tissue. Safe coverage and later local control need assessment beyond placing the device.
records.summary:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.

notes: BOOSTER studied ablation added to continuing immunotherapy in selected advanced lung cancer with limited residual disease after response. It was not an SBRT trial or a comparison in every metastatic setting. Cryo-versus-heating comparisons within that small trial were exploratory rather than a randomised test of the two modalities.

Record the method, applicator settings such as power in watts, exposure time, measured temperature in degrees Celsius where relevant, and three-dimensional zone or margin measurements with the imaging method and assessment time. A generator setting or one sensor does not measure exposure everywhere or count viable cells.

BOOSTER randomised 65 selected patients with residual advanced lung cancer after checkpoint treatment, rather than the planned 137; its primary analysis included 42 with ablation and twenty without. The primary progression-free-survival clock began at immunotherapy initiation, before randomisation, so its medians of 26.7 versus 11.7 months include a selected pre-entry period. The report separately gives a randomisation-clock analysis of 17.1 versus 4.4 months. These clocks cannot be exchanged when comparing headlines. The physician selected freezing or heating: the abstract says thirteen cryoablation and 31 thermal-ablation patients, whereas Figure 3 and the discussion say thirteen and 29 among the 42 analysed. The discussion also notes larger lesions in the thermal group and no correction for multiple comparisons. This internally discrepant, exploratory comparison does not establish universal superiority of freezing or an immune-optimal modality.

Colorectal metastases: NICE NG151 says to consider chemotherapy with local ablative techniques for colorectal liver metastases unsuitable for liver resection, and to consider metastasectomy, ablation or stereotactic body radiation therapy for lung metastases suitable for local treatment after discussion by a multidisciplinary team that includes a thoracic surgeon and a specialist in non-surgical ablation.

records.name: Phase 1, 2 and 3 trials
records.tldr: Phase 1 studies dosage and safety; phase 3 compares treatments, often in hundreds or thousands of participants. The protocol determines the design and size, and a phase 3 label is not approval or a promise of benefit.
records.summary: Clinical-trial phases describe development purposes rather than a fixed sample size, assignment method or promise of benefit. Phase 1 studies administration, exposure, safety and dosage, sometimes with early activity measures. Phase 2 asks whether activity and safety support further study in a specified population. Phase 3 compares with a defined alternative and can provide evidence for an approval decision; a phase 3 label is not itself approval. FDA's patient overview illustrates phase 3 with hundreds to thousands of participants, while the actual size follows the protocol's question and information requirements. Phase 4 studies an approved treatment in broader use. Read the protocol because phases can overlap or be combined.

notes: A phase 1 activity signal neither establishes benefit nor excludes serious toxicity. A phase 2 study may be single-arm or randomized, and phase 3 may ask superiority or a prespecified non-inferiority question. Sample size follows the question and power or information assumptions; phase number alone does not determine it. A higher phase does not guarantee that a new treatment wins or that one participant benefits. Studying an approved product in phase 4 does not approve every investigated use. A single-arm study has one intervention group; identify its actual external comparison, if any, and endpoint.

I-SPY 2 illustrates an adaptively randomized phase 2 platform. Its 2016 neratinib report describes assignment within biomarker subtypes based on Bayesian probabilities of treatment superiority over control; its veliparib-carboplatin report also describes adaptive assignment within subtype. These are properties of that platform, not every phase 2 trial. Recruitment status is another distinct question: overall recruiting status does not establish an available local cohort slot or that a particular person meets the protocol.
